text:
Chapter two. We've been here before.

Twice, in fact. Let's start with the one most people forget.

December 1989. Japan is the hottest stock market on Earth. Banks, real estate, electronics. Everyone wants in.

At its peak, Japan made up around forty-two percent of the entire global stock market.

Japanese stocks traded at around sixty times their earnings. People joked that the land under the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was worth more than all the real estate in California.

Bigger than the United States. If you bought the world in 1989, you mostly bought Japan.

The Nikkei closed that year at almost thirty-nine thousand points. It would take thirty-four years, until February 2024, to see that level again.

Today Japan is around six percent of the world index.

But here's the part almost nobody tells you. A world index investor in 1989 was not ruined.

As Japan shrank, the index automatically shifted toward everything else. In dollars, the world index was back to its 1989 level within about four years.

That's the self-cleaning feature of a market cap index. It concentrates into bubbles, but it also lets the losers shrink and the next winners grow.

Now the second time. March 2000. The internet changes everything, and investors pay any price for it.

The top ten companies are about twenty-six percent of the S and P five hundred. Valuations hit forty-four times earnings, the highest ever recorded.

For a moment in March 2000, Cisco, a company that makes network equipment, was the most valuable company in the world.

Companies with no profits went public and doubled on their first day. If it had dot com in the name, people bought it.

Then it breaks. The Nasdaq one hundred falls more than eighty percent.

It needs more than fifteen years to get back to its peak.

And no, Europe was not a safe place to hide. Telecom stocks were the European version of the bubble. The Euro Stoxx fifty lost about two thirds of its value from 2000 to 2003.

Germany had its own story. Deutsche Telekom was sold to ordinary families as the people's share. At the peak in March 2000, it traded above one hundred euros.

Two years later, it was below ten. Millions of first-time investors lost about ninety percent, and a whole generation of Germans swore off the stock market.

That's the hidden cost of a bubble. Not just the money. The people who never come back.

So let's put then and now side by side.

Share of the top ten in the S and P five hundred: about twenty-six percent then, close to forty now.

Valuations: forty-four then, around forty-one now.

And the US share of the world index: roughly half back then. More than seventy percent today.

On paper, today looks just as stretched, and more concentrated.

There is one big difference. Today's giants make enormous profits. In 2000, plenty of internet darlings had no earnings at all.

But profitable doesn't mean cheap. Cisco was very profitable in 2000. Its share price still fell by more than eighty percent.

A great company can still be a bad investment at the wrong price.
